headline: A matching prefix is a path, not just a set of letters
statement: Determine whether word can be formed by moving horizontally or vertically between adjacent board cells. A cell may be used at most once in a single path.
constraints: Board and word contain uppercase or lowercase English letters
intuition: A matching prefix is a path, not just a set of letters. Try each start, marking the cells used by that path and restoring them when the branch finishes.
approach: Reject words longer than the board or requiring more occurrences of a letter than the board supplies.
Start a depth-first search from every cell matching the first letter.
Reject out-of-bounds, used cells, or a character mismatch.
Mark a match and search its four neighbors for the next letter.
Restore the cell on both success and failure; return true if any complete path is found.
correctness: A recursive state uses only distinct adjacent cells matching exactly the prefix before its index. Each legal next cell is explored, preserving the invariant. Reaching the word length proves a valid path; exhaustive failed branches prove that no start works.
bruteForce: Enumerate all grid walks of the word length and check every completed walk for letters and repeated cells.

complexity.explanation: DFS has at most L active letters. The frequency precheck scans rows*columns cells and stores at most 52 English-letter counts; auxiliary space is O(L+52), effectively O(L).

pitfalls: A used cell is unavailable only for its current path.
Restore the board before returning success too.
